newsitem.title: USA: Exxon, FTC to settle premium gas suit out of court.
newsitem.headline: Exxon, FTC to settle premium gas suit out of court.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission said Thursday Exxon Corp has agreed to settle out of court a lawsuit over alleged advertising claims for its premium gasoline and will soon announce a new approach to keep consumers from buying the higher octane fuel.

When the FTC filed the lawsuit on September 17 Exxon said it would contest the charge, unlike previous similar suits where oil companies had agreed to tone down advertising to avoid going to court. Neither Exxon nor the FTC would say how the case was settled.
"At this point we are talking with the FTC but there is no resolution," said Exxon spokesman Dave Gardener.
Neither side would discuss terms of the proposed settlement.
The FTC filed the case as part of its effort to warn consumers against paying extra for gasoline with octane ratings above 87. The octane level is a measure of resistance to knocking.
"There is a very deeply entrenched belief that has developed over the years that high octane is better for your car," Joel Winston, FTC assistant director of advertising practices, said on Thursday.
Winston said an announcement on the settlement will be made in the next few weeks along with the federal agency's new approach to keep consumers from buying premium gasoline.
For the past several years, the FTC has been warning consumers against filling up their cars with high octane fuel through education programs, lawsuits and publicity.
"It is hard to tell how much our message is getting through," Winston said.
Exxon is the fourth major U.S. oil concern to run afoul of the FTC for making overblown claims for its high octane fuel but it was the first not to settle before a suit was filed.
According to the American Automobile Association, drivers waste about $1.7 billion a year on higher octane fuel, which it says does not provide more power, burn more clearly or improve performance.
Premium gasoline sales comprise about 20 percent of total gas sold but fewer than 10 percent of cars need it.
"People think they are giving their cars a treat. It's a myth," says AAA Director of Environment and Energy, William Berman.

The oil industry argues that 19 pecent of all U.S. vehicles need premium to assure smooth combustion and prevent knocking and ping noises associated with lower-octane fuels. In addition, a vast number of old vehicles that once used the now banned anti-knock leaded fuel need high octane to operate properly. ((-- Laney Salisbury, New York Energy Desk 1212 859-1631 --))
